summary: Analyzes the threats to the Unidirectional Lightweight Encapsulation protocol, which carries IP over MPEG-2 transport streams, and derives security requirements. It gives the motivation for link-layer security for a ULE stream. This is an informational document.

plainLanguage.summary: Sending Internet traffic through a TV signal means anyone with a dish can listen. This memo lists what could go wrong and what protections are needed.

questions: ip over mpeg-2 transport stream security
what are the security threats for ip over mpeg-2
why does ule need link-layer security
what is the difference between ule security and ipsec
how does ule protect receiver identity
subtitle: Security requirements for IP transmitted over MPEG-2 digital broadcast.

tldr.problem: MPEG-2 transport streams (used in digital TV and DVB) are broadcast over wide areas, making them vulnerable to eavesdropping and active attacks. When IP packets are carried over ULE (Unidirectional Lightweight Encapsulation) in these streams, standard IP-layer security may not be sufficient.
tldr.mechanism: This document analyzes threats in three categories (passive monitoring, local active attacks, global active attacks) and derives link-layer security requirements including mandatory confidentiality, optional integrity protection and replay protection, and optional receiver authentication.
tldr.outcome: The framework guides the design of security extensions for ULE, allowing encrypted and authenticated transport of IP over MPEG-2 without relying solely on IPsec or higher-layer security.

today: RFC 5458 remains an Informational document that guides the security design for IP over MPEG-2 networks. RFC 5163 later defined extension headers for ULE and GSE that implement these requirements. The threat analysis and security framework remain relevant for any system transmitting IP packets over broadcast MPEG-2 links, including modern DVB-based networks and satellite-delivered IP services.

sections.title: IP over MPEG-2 and Broadcast Security
sections.content:
MPEG-2 Transport Streams (TS) are standardized by ISO 13818-1 for carrying video, audio, and data. Unidirectional Lightweight Encapsulation (ULE), defined in RFC 4326, lets IP packets (IPv4 or IPv6) be carried directly as part of MPEG-2 TS Private Data. This combination is used in digital broadcast networks, DVB systems, and satellite delivery.

The problem is inherent to the broadcast nature: MPEG-2 TS is transmitted to many receivers simultaneously, often over wireless links. Unlike unicast links, a broadcast stream can be received by anyone within transmission range (not just intended recipients), making it vulnerable to passive eavesdropping. Additionally, an attacker with sufficient sophistication and access to the transmission chain might inject, modify, or replay messages.

This document performs a detailed threat analysis of IP-over-MPEG-2 networks and derives the security requirements needed to protect ULE streams. The analysis applies to both unidirectional links (broadcast to many receivers) and bidirectional links (point-to-point or two-way networks using MPEG-2 physical and link layers).
sections.plainLanguage: A TV broadcast is sent to lots of people at once. Anyone with a receiver can listen. This memo explains the threats and what tools work to protect the data.

sections.title: Threat Analysis and Attack Categories
sections.content:
The document analyzes threats in three main categories. Case 1: Passive Monitoring (eavesdropping) occurs when an attacker simply monitors the ULE broadcasts to extract data or identify communicating parties by observing Layer 2 addresses. This is a major threat in broadcast networks because receiver hardware is cheap and widely available.

Case 2: Local Active Attacks involve an attacker with physical access to a limited portion of the transmission network (e.g., a single site). The attacker can override the broadcast signal and deliver a modified version to one or a few receivers, potentially injecting forged data, replaying old messages, or modifying legitimate messages. Case 2 can involve either outsiders (attackers without knowledge of cryptographic keys) or insiders (with key knowledge).

Case 3: Global Active Attacks involve an attacker able to override the entire MPEG-2 multiplex. These are less likely in operational networks because the operator can usually detect and correct such attacks. The document focuses on Cases 1 and 2.

Active attacks include masquerading (pretending to be a legitimate source), message modification, replay attacks (resending old messages that are accepted as new), and denial-of-service attacks. In broadcast networks, replay is particularly feasible because previously transmitted data remains available to an attacker.
sections.plainLanguage: Threats include someone listening to everything (eavesdropping), someone locally sneaking in fake messages, and someone taking over the whole broadcast. The local and global takeover attacks are harder but possible.

sections.title: Security Requirements for ULE
sections.content:
From the threat analysis, the document derives five core security requirements:

Requirement 1 (mandatory): Data confidentiality MUST be provided by ULE link security. Encryption prevents passive eavesdropping and reduces the risk of active threats. Without it, anyone monitoring the broadcast sees all IP packets and their contents.

Requirement 2 (optional): Protection of Layer 2 NPA (Network Point of Attachment) addresses MAY be provided to prevent intruders from tracking which receivers are present and their traffic volume. In multicast scenarios, this is particularly valuable.

Requirement 3 (optional): Data integrity and source authentication MAY be provided using techniques like message authentication codes (MACs), digital signatures, or TESLA. These prevent Case 2 attacks where an attacker injects forged messages.

Requirement 4 (optional): Replay attack protection MAY use sequence numbers or timestamps to reject old (replayed) messages that would otherwise appear valid.

Requirement 5 (optional): Receiver authentication (either unidirectional or bidirectional) MAY be performed during initial key exchange, before the receiver can join a secure ULE session.

Beyond these, general requirements include: key management MUST be decoupled from security services, algorithm agility MUST be supported for updating cryptographic methods, the security extension header MUST be compatible with other ULE extensions, and manual or automated key insertion SHOULD be supported.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone needs encryption. Everything else is optional depending on risk. The system must be flexible enough to change encryption methods later, and must let administrators manage keys.

sections.title: Security Framework and Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
The document proposes a modular security framework with three main building blocks: a Key Management Block (for authentication and key distribution, possibly using GSAKMP or GDOI), ULE Security Databases (SAD and SPD, similar to IPsec's architecture), and a ULE Security Extension Header Block (for applying encryption and authentication to actual data).

Security can be integrated at different layers. IPsec at Layer 3 provides end-to-end security but adds overhead (extra IP headers in tunnel mode) and cannot protect Layer 2 receiver identities. MPEG-2 TS encryption below ULE encrypts all traffic with a given PID but cannot separate encryption by individual flows and requires all receivers sharing a PID to share decryption keys, risking exposure to unintended receivers' traffic. ULE link-layer security offers a middle ground: it protects individual ULE streams, can separate encryption per IP flow or receiver, allows protection of receiver identities, works efficiently with IP multicast, and does not interfere with network address translation (NAT) or performance enhancing proxies.

The framework supports multiple security profiles: a base profile (encryption and identity protection) and extended profiles adding MAC, replay protection, and authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: Three places to add locks: at the IP level (strong but heavyweight), at the broadcast level (protects everyone on a channel equally), or at the ULE level (flexible per-stream protection). ULE-level security is recommended.

sections.title: Status and Related Work
sections.content:
RFC 5458 is an Informational document that does not itself define security protocols or extension header formats. Instead, it provides guidance for future protocol design. It references RFC 4326 (ULE specification) and RFC 4259 (MPEG-2 transmission framework). RFC 5163 subsequently defined new extension headers for ULE and Generic Stream Encapsulation (GSE, used in DVB second-generation systems), and the security requirements in RFC 5458 apply to both ULE and GSE.

The document acknowledges that some security issues are explicitly out of scope: uninitialized stuffing bytes, integrity of frame removal in bridged environments, and length field validation. End-to-end security mechanisms like IPsec, TLS, or SSH should still be used by applications requiring strong authentication of endpoints. ULE link-layer security is intended as a complement to, not replacement for, these mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo explains what you need, not how to build it. Other RFCs built the actual tools. The memo helps operators and engineers decide what level of protection to add.
